title: Performance: where compiled code wins and how it was measured
summary: Gains come from not tokenising, routing calls directly, and the IBM REXX/370 compiler's techniques (Tom Dyer's brief): stems as arrays, loop counters as machine integers, whole-number operators on int64, native registers. Tight-loop bench native/bench/loops.rex: 4.49 s to 0.26 s compiled against 1.55 s interpreted. The compiler compiling itself: native 250 s, interpreted 344 s (fixed point at cd77a49). Josep Maria Blasco's Rexx Parser benchmark (pbench2.rex) at main e3d8d00 (2026-10-26): dump pass 50.5 s interpreted against 17.7 s compiled, three passes 144.8 s against 54.1 s (2.68x), dumps identical; 79,398 trips to the interpreter a pass (about 1% of the time; at 61285d6: 135.3 s against 55.0 s, 90,193 trips); his own rebuild at ca25535 was identical over 171,372 elements. Crossings (calls between compiled code and the interpreter) can dominate when compiled code works on interpreter objects, but on pbench2 they are about 1%: count and sample before optimising.
invariants: Every fast path keeps the interpreter's results byte for byte; it checks its case at run time and otherwise falls back.
Time on an idle machine, one build or run at a time; report interpreted and compiled side by side.
Report numbers with the commit they were measured on.

A trip to the interpreter (a message to an interpreter object) costs about 2.3 us from compiled code against under 1 us inside the interpreter: each API call takes the kernel lock. Read String results in place (stringFields), never add API calls to a hot path, count trips with RX2CPP_BIF_STATS=1.
